title: The empty square (2020)
hook: in the pandemic, Francis prays alone in the rain in St Peter's Square
carry: we are in the same boat

segments.voice: Yesterday, human fraternity: a pope and a Grand Imam signing one document in Abu Dhabi. Your line was brothers and sisters. Whose name did you use in a greeting? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

Evening. Rain on the stones. St Peter's Square, built to hold huge crowds, is completely empty. The city is locked down; a virus is moving through the world, and people are dying in hospitals without their families beside them. Up the wide steps, under a canopy, one figure in white walks slowly, alone. No crowd answers him. Cameras carry the picture into kitchens and living rooms and hospital break rooms around the world. The pope has come out to pray, for a world that can't come to him. And the reading he chose is about a boat in a storm.
screen: `RAIN, AND AN EMPTY SQUARE.` → `ONE FIGURE IN WHITE.` → `A BOAT IN A STORM.`

segments.voice: The service was plain, and each piece of it was chosen. First, the reading. Mark's Gospel tells of the disciples crossing the lake at night when a great storm comes up and the waves pour into the boat. Jesus is asleep in the stern on a cushion. They wake him, and in the Douay-Rheims they say: "Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" He calms the wind, and then asks them: "Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Second, what Francis heard in it. In his homily he said the storm had shown that we are all in the same boat, fragile and disoriented, and all needing each other. The storm, he said, strips away the comfortable things we use to look secure. He didn't say the storm was a punishment. He said everyone was in it. Third, what stood beside him. A wooden crucifix from a church in Rome, which tradition says was once carried through the streets in a time of plague, stood out in the rain. And an icon of Mary from a Roman basilica. Fourth, the blessing. At the end he held up the Eucharist in a monstrance and gave the blessing the popes call to the city and to the world, over an empty square, to everyone watching wherever they were. Bells rang. Sirens could be heard in the distance. The picture is plain: a man alone in the rain, praying for people he would never meet, many of them dying alone.
screen: `THE STORM AND THE SLEEPING JESUS.` · `ALL IN THE SAME BOAT.` · `A CRUCIFIX AND AN ICON IN THE RAIN.` · `A BLESSING OVER AN EMPTY SQUARE.` · then, large: `WHY ARE YOU FEARFUL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those who died alone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who died in those months without a hand to hold. You may know some by name. If you do, let their names come one at a time. If not, think of a hospital corridor at night, a nurse holding up a phone so a family can say goodbye. Stay with them. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for the nurses and doctors who stood in for families. If you don't, simply remember them. The bell holds the time.
Monstrance. The vessel in which Pope Francis held up the Eucharist to bless the city and the world, alone in the rain over an empty St Peter's Square.
Your line: we are in the same boat. Today, check in on someone who spent those months alone, and ask how they're doing now. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dead at every Mass and in November especially, and the blessing Urbi et Orbi is usually given by the pope at Christmas and Easter, and on rare occasions like this one.

what a scholar hears: a blessing Urbi et Orbi with the Eucharist, given outside its usual feasts, to a square with no one in it.

notes: Claims rule: no date spoken. 'Limping a little', 'sirens could be heard', 'bells rang' and 'people... still describe the silence' are descriptive details from coverage, not the cited text; Keeper may cut any of them.

Homily paraphrase: 'we are all in the same boat, all of us fragile and disoriented', the storm exposing false securities, and that he did not frame it as punishment (he spoke of it as a time of choosing, not God's judgment): confirm.
San Marcello crucifix 'carried through the streets in a time of plague' is given as 'tradition says'; Salus Populi Romani icon described without naming; confirm.
'Romans have long prayed before' the icon is a soft historical claim; Keeper may cut.
howItsDone: confirm Urbi et Orbi is usually given at Christmas and Easter (and after election).
Mark 4:38 and 4:40 Douay-Rheims wording: confirm exactly (verse numbering may differ by one in some editions).

Editor: cut 'limping', the garbled 'people who were there on screen still describe the silence' and the 'picture lasts' claim; 'Romans have long prayed before' became 'from a Roman basilica'; varied the teach opener.
Auditor: read in full; Mark 4:38 and 4:40 match the Douay-Rheims (which says Jesus slept on a pillow; the voice paraphrases as cushion); no change.
